channel.title: W3C Web Application Security Working Group-relevant MDN issues
channel.description: Issue filed on MDN Web Docs related to pages attached to technologies developed by W3C Web Application Security Working Group

item.title: [credential-management-1] FedCM API's description of the returned IdentityCredential is inaccurate
item.content:encoded:
In the FedCM API, the RP calls navigator.credentials.get(), and if all goes well gets back an IdentityCredential object.

MDN's documentation for this operation and the returned object indicates that the IdentityCredential contains a token signed with the IdP's key, and that the RP needs to verify the signature, and if it's correct, can sign the user in. See e.g. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/FedCM_API/RP_sign-in:

The method returns a promise that fulfills with an IdentityCredential object if the user identity is successfully validated by the chosen IdP. This object contains a token that includes user identity information that has been signed with the IdP's digital certificate.

The RP sends the token to its server to validate the certificate, and on success can use the (now trusted) identity information in the token to sign them into their service (starting a new session), sign them up to their service if they are a new user, etc.

But the FedCM API makes no promises at all about what the returned token contains or what the RP needs to do with it:

The content of the token is opaque to the user agent and can contain anything that the IDP would like to pass to the RP to facilitate the login. For this reason the RP is expected to be the party responsible for validating the token passed along from the IDP using the appropriate token validation algorithms defined.

(https://w3c-fedid.github.io/FedCM/#idp-api-id-assertion-endpoint)

In particular, in the OAuth/OIDC profile for FedCM (w3c-fedid/FedCM#599), the token in the IdentityCredential is an OAuth "authorization code", which the RP has to send back to the IdP to get the actual signed identity/access token. That is, FedCM only gets you through the first step of the two-step OAuth "authorization code flow" that's recommended for OAuth/OIDC clients.

w3c-fedid/FedCM#536 is also interesting here.

The FedCM docs should say:

  1. what the returned token is, per spec (anything at all)
  2. how RPs should figure out what to do with it (follow the IdP's instructions)
  3. some common things it might be, depending on which protocol the IdP is using and in what way (e.g. an authorization code, if they were using the OAuth/OIDC profile linked above).

item.title: [referrer-policy] Add information to Referrer-Policy docs about how it can affect the Origin header
item.content:encoded:
MDN URL

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Referrer-Policy

What specific section or headline is this issue about?

No response

What information was incorrect, unhelpful, or incomplete?

When reading through this page, I don't see any references to how the Referrer-Policy settings may affect the origin header. It sounds as though it only affects the referer header, but it can also affect the origin header.

What did you expect to see?

In the description for the origin header, it mentions that origin may be set to null depending on the value of referr-policy.

The Origin header value may be null in a number of cases, including (non-exhaustively):

  • ...
  • Referrer-Policy set to no-referrer for non-cors request modes (e.g. simple form posts).

When choosing a referrer-policy, I wasn't aware of this side-effect. It would be really helpful to mention this clearly on this page as well, or at least link back to the Origin docs.

Do you have any supporting links, references, or citations?

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Origin#description

Do you have anything more you want to share?

I'd be happy to start a PR but it may take a bit of time to make sure it's accurate. I would need to understand more clearly in which cases the origin header is affected and how. I would guess it's not just for no-referrer but also for some cross origin requests or e.g. no-referrer-when-downgrade. Also I'd imagine this can vary by browser.
